claim: Betulin is a key bioactive compound in aphid-resistant wild peach (Prunus davidiana).
source: Betulin, a key bioactive compound in aphid-resistant wild peach, possesses promising applications in crop protection.
evidence: Referenced in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work (Wang et al., 2022a; Wang et al., 2024) in the introduction.

claim: Betulin displayed excellent control efficacy against Myzus persicae in both greenhouse and field experiments.
source: Here, betulin, in both greenhouse and field experiments, displayed excellent control efficacy against Myzus persicae.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 showing control efficacy in greenhouse and field tests.

claim: Betulin significantly inhibited the expression of MpGABR (encoding a GABAA receptor).
source: RNA-seq, quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), and western blotting revealed that betulin significantly inhibited the expression of MpGABR (encoding a GABAA receptor).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq, qRT-PCR, and western blotting data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of MpGABR markedly increased aphid sensitivity to betulin.
source: Besides, RNAi-mediated silencing of MpGABR markedly increased aphid sensitivity to betulin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing increased mortality after MpGABR silencing.

claim: Betulin bound to MpGABR with a Kd of 2.24 µM.
source: Furthermore, microscale thermophoresis (MST) and voltage-clamp assays indicated that betulin bound to MpGABR (Kd = 2.24 µM) and acted as an inhibitor of MpGABR.
evidence: Supported by MST experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Betulin acted as an inhibitor of MpGABR with an EC50 of 20.66 µM.
source: Furthermore, microscale thermophoresis (MST) and voltage-clamp assays indicated that betulin bound to MpGABR (Kd = 2.24 µM) and acted as an inhibitor of MpGABR.
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp assay data showing EC50 value in Figure 6D.

claim: THR228 is a critical and highly conserved site in MpGABR that betulin binds to specifically.
source: Molecular docking, mutagenesis, and genome editing suggested that THR228 is a critical and highly conserved site in MpGABR that betulin binds to specifically, causing aphid death.
evidence: Supported by molecular docking data (Figure 7A), sequence alignment (Figure 7B), mutagenesis experiments (Figure 7D-E), and genome editing experiments (Figure 8).

claim: The LC50 value of betulin against M. persicae at 48 hr was 0.1641 mg⋅mL–1.
source: Bioassays revealed that the LC50 values of betulin and pymetrozine against M. persicae at 48 hr were 0.1641 and 1.0612 mg⋅mL–1, respectively (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by bioassay data referenced in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The LC50 value of pymetrozine against M. persicae at 48 hr was 1.0612 mg⋅mL–1.
source: Bioassays revealed that the LC50 values of betulin and pymetrozine against M. persicae at 48 hr were 0.1641 and 1.0612 mg⋅mL–1, respectively (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by bioassay data referenced in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: After 14 days of treatment in the greenhouse, the control efficacy of betulin against M. persicae reached 91.54%.
source: After 14 days of treatment, the control efficacies of betulin and pymetrozine reached 91.54% and 95.15%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by greenhouse test data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: After 14 days of treatment in the greenhouse, the control efficacy of pymetrozine against M. persicae reached 95.15%.
source: After 14 days of treatment, the control efficacies of betulin and pymetrozine reached 91.54% and 95.15%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by greenhouse test data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: After 14 days of treatment in the field, the control efficacy of betulin against M. persicae was 87.79%.
source: Throughout the field test (Figure 1F), no difference in the control efficacy was observed between betulin and pymetrozine, with values of 87.79% and 90.14%, respectively, after 14 days of treatment (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by field test data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: After 14 days of treatment in the field, the control efficacy of pymetrozine against M. persicae was 90.14%.
source: Throughout the field test (Figure 1F), no difference in the control efficacy was observed between betulin and pymetrozine, with values of 87.79% and 90.14%, respectively, after 14 days of treatment (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by field test data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There were 130 upregulated and 41 downregulated significant differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in M. persicae after betulin treatment compared with the control group.
source: Compared with those in the CK group, there were 130 up- and 41 downregulated significant differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in M. persicae after betulin treatment (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The DEGs were enriched mainly in the GABAA receptor activity term according to GO term enrichment analysis.
source: GO term enrichment demonstrated that the DEGs were enriched mainly in the GABAA receptor activity term (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: KEGG enrichment found that the DEGs were enriched in the GABAergic signaling-related pathway and GABAergic synapse terms.
source: Interestingly, KEGG enrichment also found that the DEGs were enriched in the GABAergic signaling-related pathway and GABAergic synapse terms (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by KEGG enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The log2(fold change) value of MpGABR was the lowest at –3.8 among GABR-related genes.
source: In particular, the log2(fold change) value of MpGABR was the lowest, at –3.8 (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data referenced in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: MpGABR protein has 694 amino acids with a calculated molecular weight of 77.20 kDa and an isoelectric point of 9.85.
source: Analysis of the sequence information revealed that the MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB proteins have 694, 118, and 250 amino acids, respectively, with calculated molecular weights of 77.20, 14.08, and 28.01 kDa and isoelectric points of 9.85, 9.63, and 7.20, respectively (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis data referenced in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: MpGABRAP protein has 118 amino acids with a calculated molecular weight of 14.08 kDa and an isoelectric point of 9.63.
source: Analysis of the sequence information revealed that the MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB proteins have 694, 118, and 250 amino acids, respectively, with calculated molecular weights of 77.20, 14.08, and 28.01 kDa and isoelectric points of 9.85, 9.63, and 7.20, respectively (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis data referenced in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: MpGABRB protein has 250 amino acids with a calculated molecular weight of 28.01 kDa and an isoelectric point of 7.20.
source: Analysis of the sequence information revealed that the MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB proteins have 694, 118, and 250 amino acids, respectively, with calculated molecular weights of 77.20, 14.08, and 28.01 kDa and isoelectric points of 9.85, 9.63, and 7.20, respectively (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis data referenced in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: MpGABR contains 4 transmembrane helical domains.
source: Additionally, structure prediction indicated that MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB contain 4, 0, and 1 transmembrane helical domain, respectively (Figure 3A), implying that only MpGABR has a complete transmembrane structure.
evidence: Supported by structure prediction data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MpGABRAP contains 0 transmembrane helical domains.
source: Additionally, structure prediction indicated that MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB contain 4, 0, and 1 transmembrane helical domain, respectively (Figure 3A), implying that only MpGABR has a complete transmembrane structure.
evidence: Supported by structure prediction data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MpGABRB contains 1 transmembrane helical domain.
source: Additionally, structure prediction indicated that MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB contain 4, 0, and 1 transmembrane helical domain, respectively (Figure 3A), implying that only MpGABR has a complete transmembrane structure.
evidence: Supported by structure prediction data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: After exposure to the LC30 of betulin for 48 hr, the relative expression of MpGABR decreased by 82.91%.
source: After exposure to the LC30 of betulin for 48 hr, the relative expression of MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB decreased by 82.91%, 10.53%, and 11.49%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After exposure to the LC30 of betulin for 48 hr, the relative expression of MpGABRAP decreased by 10.53%.
source: After exposure to the LC30 of betulin for 48 hr, the relative expression of MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB decreased by 82.91%, 10.53%, and 11.49%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After exposure to the LC30 of betulin for 48 hr, the relative expression of MpGABRB decreased by 11.49%.
source: After exposure to the LC30 of betulin for 48 hr, the relative expression of MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB decreased by 82.91%, 10.53%, and 11.49%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Compared with the control group, the MpGABR protein content in M. persicae exposed to betulin at LC30, LC50, and LC70 decreased by 33.68%, 44.89%, and 76.89%, respectively.
source: Compared with that in the CK group, the MpGABR protein content in M. persicae exposed to betulin concentrations of LC30, LC50, and LC70 decreased by 33.68%, 44.89%, and 76.89%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: After RNAi, the expression levels of MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB in M. persicae significantly decreased by 64.57%, 63.28%, and 67.33%, respectively, compared with control groups.
source: Furthermore, after these three genes were silenced via RNAi (Figure 4D), the expression levels of MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB in M. persicae significantly decreased by 64.57%, 63.28%, and 67.33%, respectively, compared with those in the control groups (DEPC-treated water and dsGFP) (p<0.0001, Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: After exposure to the LC50 of betulin for 48 hr, the mortality of M. persicae with MpGABR silenced markedly increased by 30.44% compared with control groups.
source: After exposure to the LC50 of betulin for 48 hr, the mortality of M. persicae with MpGABR silenced markedly increased (p<0.001) by 30.44%, compared with that in the control groups, whereas the mortalities of M. persicae in the MpGABRAP- and MpGABRB-silenced groups did not significantly differ from that in the control groups (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by mortality data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: MpGABR protein expression significantly decreased by 69.91% after RNAi.
source: Additionally, western blotting analysis revealed that MpGABR protein expression significantly decreased by 69.91% after RNAi (p<0.0001, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: MpGABR (XP_022173711.1) was found to be genetically closely related to CAI6365831.1 from Macrosiphum euphorbiae, XP 008183008.2 from Acyrthosiphon pisum, and XP 060864885.1 from Metopolophium dirhodum.
source: MpGABR (XP_022173711.1) was found to be genetically closely related to CAI6365831.1 from Macrosiphum euphorbiae, XP 008183008.2 from Acyrthosiphon pisum, and XP 060864885.1 from Metopolophium dirhodum (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that MpGABR may be functionally analogous to CAI6365831.1, XP 008183008.2, and XP 060864885.1.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The predicted binding energy between betulin and MpGABR was −6.38 kcal⋅mol–1.
source: The docking results revealed that the predicted binding energy between betulin and MpGABR was −6.38 kcal⋅mol–1 (Figure 7—source data 1), verifying that betulin could act as a specific ligand for MpGABR.
evidence: Supported by molecular docking data referenced in Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: Four key amino acid residues (ARG224, ALA226, PHE227, and THR228) interacted with betulin in the MpGABR binding pocket.
source: The three-dimensional binding pattern of betulin with MpGABR indicated that the four key amino acid residues (ARG224, ALA226, PHE227, and THR228) interacted with betulin in the MpGABR binding pocket (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by molecular docking data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: ALA226 and THR228 interacted with betulin via hydrogen bonding in the MpGABR binding pocket.
source: Among the four key amino acid residues, ALA226 and THR228 interacted with betulin via hydrogen bonding in the MpGABR binding pocket (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by molecular docking data referenced in Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: Betulin generated nonconventional H-bonds (C…H) with ALA226 at 3.31 Å.
source: Betulin generated nonconventional H-bonds (C…H) with ALA226 (3.31  Å) and conventional H-bonds (C-O H) with THR228 (2.16 Å).
evidence: Supported by molecular docking data.

claim: Betulin generated conventional H-bonds (C-O H) with THR228 at 2.16 Å.
source: Betulin generated nonconventional H-bonds (C…H) with ALA226 (3.31  Å) and conventional H-bonds (C-O H) with THR228 (2.16 Å).
evidence: Supported by molecular docking data.

claim: THR228 was conserved across 11 species in the Aphididae family of Hemiptera.
source: Furthermore, sequence alignment of the key amino acid residues of GABR in different species from Hemiptera, Diptera, Lepidoptera, Hymenoptera, Thysanoptera, and Coleoptera indicated that, among the four residues, only THR228 was conserved across 11 species in the Aphididae family of Hemiptera (Figure 7B), implying that THR228 may be an essential specific site for the action of betulin on MpGABR in aphids.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Kd values of R224A, A226T, F227Y, T228R, and WT MpGABR mutants with betulin were 2.31, 2.27, 2.25, 5321, and 2.24 μM, respectively.
source: The results revealed that the Kd values of R224A, A226T, F227Y, T228R, and WT were 2.31, 2.27, 2.25, 5321, and 2.24 μM, respectively (Figure 7D and E, Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by MST data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The mutation at the THR228 site markedly reduced the binding ability of betulin to MpGABR.
source: This result suggested that the mutation at the THR228 site, with the highest Kd value, markedly reduced the binding ability of betulin to MpGABR, implying that the THR228 site may be an essential specific site for the binding of betulin to MpGABR.
evidence: Inferred from the Kd values of mutants shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Betulin was able to bind to DmGABRR122T (Kd = 342.4 µM) but not to DmGABRWT.
source: As shown in Figure 8B, betulin was able to bind to DmGABRR122T (Kd = 342.4 µM) but not to DmGABRWT.
evidence: Supported by MST data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Pymetrozine exhibited no binding affinity for DmGABRR122T or DmGABRWT.
source: However, pymetrozine exhibited no binding affinity for DmGABRR122T or DmGABRWT (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by MST data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: After exposure to different concentrations of betulin, the mortality rate of DmGABRR122T Drosophila was significantly greater than that of DmGABRWT Drosophila.
source: Moreover, to generate Drosophila mutant individuals carrying DmGABRR122T, the CRISPR/Cas9 genomic editing strategy was used. After exposure to different concentrations of betulin, the mortality rate of DmGABRR122T Drosophila was significantly greater than that of DmGABRWT Drosophila (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by toxicity data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The LD50 value of betulin against DmGABRR122T Drosophila at 72 hr was 27.19 μg⋅fly−1.
source: In addition, the LD50 value of betulin against DmGABRR122T Drosophila at 72 hr was 27.19 μg⋅fly−1, whereas the LD50 value of betulin against DmGABRWT Drosophila could not be calculated because the lethal concentration exceeded 1000 μg⋅fly−1 (Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by toxicity data referenced in Figure 8—source data 1.

claim: There was no significant difference in mortality between DmGABRWT and DmGABRR122T Drosophila after exposure to pymetrozine.
source: Additionally, there was no significant difference in mortality between DmGABRWT and DmGABRR122T Drosophila after exposure to pymetrozine (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by toxicity data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The LD50 values of pymetrozine against DmGABRWT and DmGABRR122T Drosophila at 72 hr were 0.23 and 0.24 μg⋅fly−1, respectively.
source: The LD50 values of pymetrozine against DmGABRWT and DmGABRR122T Drosophila at 72 hr were 0.23 and 0.24 μg⋅fly−1, respectively (Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by toxicity data referenced in Figure 8—source data 1.

claim: THR228 is located at the neurotransmitter-gated ion-channel ligand-binding domain in MpGABR.
source: Moreover, THR228 is located at the neurotransmitter-gated ion-channel ligand-binding domain in MpGABR (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), implying that betulin may play a role as a competitive antagonist of MpGABR.
evidence: Supported by protein structure data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Betulin bound specifically to MpGABR via THR228, resulting in the death of M. persicae.
source: Taken together, these findings suggested that betulin bound specifically to MpGABR via THR228, resulting in the death of M. persicae.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including mutagenesis, MST, and genome editing data.

claim: Myzus persicae is able to settle on more than 400 plant species globally.
source: It is able to settle on more than 400 plant species globally, displaying extraordinary polyphagia and a wide range of hazards (Bass et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bass et al., 2014.

claim: M. persicae can transmit various plant viruses.
source: In addition to ingesting phloem saps and secreting honeydew, M. persicae can transmit various plant viruses (Guo et al., 2022), resulting in severe losses in crop yields.
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2022.

claim: Long-term irrational application of chemical insecticides has led to environmental pollution and promoted the resistance of aphids to insecticides.
source: However, long-term irrational application of these chemical insecticides has led to environmental pollution and promoted the resistance of aphids to insecticides (Troczka et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023; Stará et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Troczka et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023; Stará et al., 2024.

claim: Prunus davidiana displays strong resistance to M. persicae through the accumulation of high levels of betulin.
source: Our previous study revealed that Prunus davidiana, a close wild relative of cultivated peach, displays strong resistance to M. persicae through the accumulation of high levels of betulin (Wang et al., 2022a; Wang et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2022a; Wang et al., 2024.

claim: Betulin and its derivatives exhibit a wide range of pharmacological activities.
source: A number of studies have reported that betulin and its derivatives exhibit a wide range of pharmacological activities (Amiri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amiri et al., 2020.

claim: Ir-Bet, prepared using iridium complex and betulin, evoked ferritinophagy-enhanced ferroptosis, thereby activating anti-tumor immunity.
source: An immune stimulant, Ir-Bet, was prepared using iridium complex and betulin, which evoked ferritinophagy-enhanced ferroptosis, thereby activating anti-tumor immunity (Lv et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lv et al., 2023.

claim: The anti-inflammatory effect of betulin has been reported in macrophages at lymphoma sites in mice.
source: The anti-inflammatory effect of betulin has been reported in macrophages at lymphoma sites in mice (Szlasa et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Szlasa et al., 2023.

claim: Betulin has been found to improve hyperlipidemia and insulin resistance and decrease atherosclerotic plaques by inhibiting the maturation of sterol regulatory element-binding protein.
source: Betulin has been found to improve hyperlipidemia and insulin resistance and decrease atherosclerotic plaques by inhibiting the maturation of sterol regulatory element-binding protein (Tang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tang et al., 2011.

claim: Betulin and its derivatives have been found to exhibit insecticidal activity against Plutella xylostella L.
source: Additionally, betulin and its derivatives have been found to exhibit insecticidal activity against Plutella xylostella L. (Huang et al., 2025), Aedes aegypti (de Almeida Teles et al., 2024), and Drosophila melanogaster (Lee and Min, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2025.

claim: Betulin and its derivatives have been found to exhibit insecticidal activity against Aedes aegypti.
source: Additionally, betulin and its derivatives have been found to exhibit insecticidal activity against Plutella xylostella L. (Huang et al., 2025), Aedes aegypti (de Almeida Teles et al., 2024), and Drosophila melanogaster (Lee and Min, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Almeida Teles et al., 2024.

claim: Betulin and its derivatives have been found to exhibit insecticidal activity against Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Additionally, betulin and its derivatives have been found to exhibit insecticidal activity against Plutella xylostella L. (Huang et al., 2025), Aedes aegypti (de Almeida Teles et al., 2024), and Drosophila melanogaster (Lee and Min, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee and Min, 2024.

claim: GABA receptors have been confirmed to be targets of terpenoids that impair neuronal function in insect herbivores.
source: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors have been confirmed to be targets of terpenoids that impair neuronal function in insect herbivores (Guo et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2023.

claim: The first GABA receptor subunit identified in insects is encoded by Rdl, which confers resistance to dieldrin in D. melanogaster.
source: The first GABA receptor subunit identified in insects is encoded by Rdl, which confers resistance to dieldrin in D. melanogaster (Ffrench-Constant et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ffrench-Constant et al., 1991.

claim: A variety of terpenoids play roles as positive allosteric modulators or noncompetitive antagonists (NCAs) of GABAA receptors (GABRs).
source: Although a variety of terpenoids play roles as positive allosteric modulators or noncompetitive antagonists (NCAs) of GABAA receptors (GABRs) (Guo et al., 2023), whether betulin targets the GABR in M. persicae needs to be further investigated.
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2023.

claim: GABRs are heteropentameric ligand-gated ion channels in the central nervous system that conduct chloride and bicarbonate ions.
source: GABRs are heteropentameric ligand-gated ion channels in the central nervous system that conduct chloride and bicarbonate ions and are the target of numerous drugs for the treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders (Thompson, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thompson, 2024.

claim: GABRs are composed of five different types of subunits, each with four helical transmembrane domains (TM1-TM4), of which TM2 is located at the center of the pentamer and forms an ion channel.
source: GABRs are composed of five different types of subunits, each with four helical transmembrane domains (TM1-TM4), of which TM2 is located at the center of the pentamer and forms an ion channel (Fan et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fan et al., 2024.

claim: Vertebrate and human GABR genes maintain a broad and conservative gene clustering pattern, while in invertebrates, this pattern is missing.
source: A previous study has proposed that vertebrate and human GABR genes maintain a broad and conservative gene clustering pattern, while in invertebrates, this pattern is missing, indicating that these gene clusters were formed early in vertebrate evolution and were established after invertebrates diverged.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsang et al., 2007.

claim: Invertebrates each possess a unique GABR gene pair, which is homologous with human GABR α and β subunits.
source: Notably, invertebrates each possess a unique GABR gene pair, which is homologous with human GABR α and β subunits, suggesting that the existing GABR gene cluster evolved from an ancestral α-β subunit gene pair (Tsang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsang et al., 2007.

claim: During the coevolution of plants and insects, the duplications and amino acid substitutions in GABR may have been beneficial for adaptation to insecticides and terpenoid compounds.
source: During the coevolution of plants and insects, the duplications and amino acid substitutions in GABR may have been beneficial for adaptation to insecticides and terpenoid compounds (Guo et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2023.

claim: Betulin has immense potential for development as a commercial aphid insecticide like pymetrozine.
source: These results suggest that betulin has immense potential for development as a commercial aphid insecticide like pymetrozine.
evidence: Inferred from the comparable control efficacy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: MpGABR may be a candidate target for betulin against M. persicae.
source: These results suggested that MpGABR may be a candidate target for betulin against M. persicae.
evidence: Inferred from RNA-seq, GO, and KEGG enrichment data showing MpGABR involvement.

claim: Only MpGABR has a complete transmembrane structure among MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB.

claim: MpGABR was the most sensitive to betulin among MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB.
source: These results indicated that MpGABR was the most sensitive to betulin.

claim: MpGABR might be a target for betulin against M. persicae.
source: These results further implied that MpGABR might be a target for betulin against M. persicae.

source: MpGABR (XP_022173711.1) was found to be genetically closely related to CAI6365831.1 from Macrosiphum euphorbiae, XP 008183008.2 from Acyrthosiphon pisum, and XP 060864885.1 from Metopolophium dirhodum (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that MpGABR may be functionally analogous to CAI6365831.1, XP 008183008.2, and XP 060864885.1.

claim: Betulin could act as a specific ligand for MpGABR.
source: The docking results revealed that the predicted binding energy between betulin and MpGABR was −6.38 kcal⋅mol–1 (Figure 7—source data 1), verifying that betulin could act as a specific ligand for MpGABR.

claim: THR228 may be an essential specific site for the action of betulin on MpGABR in aphids.
source: Furthermore, sequence alignment of the key amino acid residues of GABR in different species from Hemiptera, Diptera, Lepidoptera, Hymenoptera, Thysanoptera, and Coleoptera indicated that, among the four residues, only THR228 was conserved across 11 species in the Aphididae family of Hemiptera (Figure 7B), implying that THR228 may be an essential specific site for the action of betulin on MpGABR in aphids.
evidence: Inferred from conservation pattern across aphid species.

claim: The THR228 site may be an essential specific site for the binding of betulin to MpGABR.

evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis data showing reduced binding when THR228 is mutated.

claim: Betulin may play a role as a competitive antagonist of MpGABR.

claim: Betulin is speculated to be a specific insecticidal substance evolved by plants in response to aphid infestation.
source: Therefore, betulin is speculated to be a specific insecticidal substance evolved by plants in response to aphid infestation.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the conservation of THR228 only in aphids.

claim: The aphicidal effects of betulin on aphids occur in a two-pronged manner: betulin inhibits MpGABR expression and specifically binds to MpGABR via THR228 and acts as an inhibitor of MpGABR.
source: Collectively, the results suggest that the aphicidal effects of betulin on aphids occur in a two-pronged manner: on the one hand, betulin inhibits MpGABR expression; on the other hand, it specifically binds to MpGABR via THR228 and acts as an inhibitor of MpGABR.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing both expression inhibition and direct binding.

claim: The control efficacy of betulin against M. persicae was significantly greater than that of pymetrozine at 1 day after treatment in the greenhouse test.
source: The control efficacy of betulin against M. persicae was significantly greater than that of pymetrozine at 1 day after treatment (p<0.01), while there were no significant differences between the control efficacies of betulin and pymetrozine at 5, 9, or 14 days after treatment (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by greenhouse test data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There were no significant differences between the control efficacies of betulin and pymetrozine at 5, 9, or 14 days after treatment in the greenhouse test.
source: The control efficacy of betulin against M. persicae was significantly greater than that of pymetrozine at 1 day after treatment (p<0.01), while there were no significant differences between the control efficacies of betulin and pymetrozine at 5, 9, or 14 days after treatment (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by greenhouse test data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No difference in the control efficacy was observed between betulin and pymetrozine throughout the field test.
source: Throughout the field test (Figure 1F), no difference in the control efficacy was observed between betulin and pymetrozine, with values of 87.79% and 90.14%, respectively, after 14 days of treatment (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by field test data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The relative expression trends of 15 randomly selected DEGs determined via qRT-PCR were similar to those detected via RNA-seq.
source: To validate the RNA-seq results, 15 DEGs were randomly selected with different expression levels. The relative expression trends of the 15 DEGs determined via qRT-PCR were similar to those detected via RNA-seq, supporting the reliability of the RNA-seq data (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The relative expression of all three GABR-related genes (MpGABR, MpGABRAP, and MpGABRB) decreased gradually as the concentration of betulin increased.
source: To further verify the inhibitory effect of betulin on GABR-related gene expression, the relative expression of the three GABR-related genes was detected in M. persicae exposed to the LC30, LC50, and LC70 of betulin for 48 hr. The relative expression of all three genes decreased gradually as the concentration of betulin increased (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: As the concentration of betulin increased, the MpGABR protein content in M. persicae gradually decreased.
source: To further investigate the effect of betulin on the MpGABR protein, M. persicae was exposed to betulin concentrations of LC30, LC50, and LC70 for 48 hr. As the concentration of betulin increased, the MpGABR protein content in M. persicae gradually decreased (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The mortalities of M. persicae in the MpGABRAP- and MpGABRB-silenced groups did not significantly differ from that in the control groups after exposure to betulin.
source: After exposure to the LC50 of betulin for 48 hr, the mortality of M. persicae with MpGABR silenced markedly increased (p<0.001) by 30.44%, compared with that in the control groups, whereas the mortalities of M. persicae in the MpGABRAP- and MpGABRB-silenced groups did not significantly differ from that in the control groups (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by mortality data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In the presence of only GABA, a fast inward current was generated in MpGABR.
source: In the presence of only GABA, a fast inward current was generated.
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: As the concentration of added betulin increased, the current and channel activity of MpGABR decreased correspondingly.
source: As the concentration of added betulin increased, the current and channel activity of MpGABR decreased correspondingly, with an EC50 value of 20.66 µM (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Betulin acted as an inhibitor of MpGABR.
source: These results indicated that betulin acted as an inhibitor of MpGABR.
evidence: Inferred from voltage-clamp data showing decreased channel activity with betulin.

claim: Betulin could bind to MpGABR.
source: The Kd value was 2.24 µM (Figure 6B), suggesting that betulin could bind to MpGABR.
evidence: Inferred from MST data showing binding affinity.

claim: Betulin has been reported to be able to bind to GABRs.
source: Additionally, betulin has been reported to be able to bind to GABRs (Manayi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manayi et al., 2016.

claim: Betulin binds to GABA receptors in mouse brains in vitro.
source: The MST assay revealed that betulin was able to bind to MpGABR (Kd = 2.24 µM) (Figure 6B), which is consistent with previous findings showing that betulin binds to GABA receptors in mouse brains in vitro (Muceniece et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muceniece et al., 2008.

claim: Betulinic acid and its derivatives showed larvicidal activity against A. aegypti larvae.
source: Betulinic acid and its derivatives showed larvicidal activity against A. aegypti larvae (da Silva et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to da Silva et al., 2016.

claim: Betulin-cinnamic acid-related hybrid compound 5b exhibited strong aphicidal activity.
source: Betulin-cinnamic acid-related hybrid compound 5b exhibited strong aphicidal activity, and compound 2l could destroy the ultrastructure of midgut cells and significantly inhibit the activity of α-amylase in diamondback moth (Pl. xylostella L.) larvae (Huang et al.).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al.

claim: Compound 2l could destroy the ultrastructure of midgut cells and significantly inhibit the activity of α-amylase in diamondback moth larvae.

claim: Diterpenoids (isopimaric acid and miltirone), sesquiterpenoids (picrotoxin, bilobalide, and ginkgolides), and monoterpenoids (α-thujone and thymol) act as positive allosteric modulators or NCAs of GABRs.
source: A variety of terpenoids act as positive allosteric modulators or NCAs of GABRs, such as diterpenoids (isopimaric acid and miltirone), sesquiterpenoids (picrotoxin, bilobalide, and ginkgolides), and monoterpenoids (α-thujone and thymol) (Guo et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2023.

claim: Epileptic seizures increase the levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor in adult rats, which in turn prompted the transcription factors CREB and ICER to reduce the gene expression of the GABR α1 subunit.
source: In adult rats, epileptic seizures have been reported to increase the levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which in turn prompted the transcription factors CREB and ICER to reduce the gene expression of the GABR α1 subunit (Lund et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lund et al., 2008.

claim: WIDE AWAKE, which regulated the onset of sleep, interacted with the GABR and upregulated its expression level in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, it has been demonstrated that WIDE AWAKE, which regulated the onset of sleep, interacted with the GABR and upregulated its expression level (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Circular RNA circ_sxc inhibits the expression of miR-87-3-p in the Drosophila brain through sponge adsorption, thereby regulating the expression of neurotransmitter receptor ligand proteins, including GABR.
source: In the Drosophila brain, circular RNA circ_sxc was found to inhibit the expression of miR-87-3-p in the brain through sponge adsorption, thereby regulating the expression of neurotransmitter receptor ligand proteins, including GABR, and ensuring the normal function of synaptic signal transmission in brain neurons (Li et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2024.

claim: The R122G amino acid site substitution, generated via RNA editing, affects the sensitivity of Drosophila to fipronil.

evidence: Supported by citation to Es-Salah et al., 2008.

evidence: Supported by citation to Nakao and Banba, 2021.

evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2023.

claim: After GABA binds to the extracellular Cys-loop of a GABR, the GABR is activated and opens up its central pore to allow chloride ions to pass through, thereby hyperpolarizing neurons and attenuating excitatory neurotransmission.
source: After GABA binds to the extracellular Cys-loop of a GABR (Ashby et al., 2012), the GABR is activated and opens up its central pore to allow chloride ions to pass through, thereby hyperpolarizing neurons and attenuating excitatory neurotransmission (Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ashby et al., 2012 and Tremblay et al., 2016.

claim: GABRs play important roles in circadian rhythms in insects.
source: In insects, GABRs play important roles in circadian rhythms (Schellinger et al., 2022), sleep (Chaturvedi et al., 2022), movement (Eick et al., 2022), and olfactory memory (Yamagata et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schellinger et al., 2022.

claim: NCAs block chloride channels in nerve cells by interacting with amino acid residues of the GABA-gated chloride channel, causing a conformational change in the receptor.
source: NCAs block chloride channels in nerve cells by interacting with amino acid residues of the GABA-gated chloride channel, causing a conformational change in the receptor, which interferes with the normal function of the central nervous system and ultimately leads to insect death (Nakao and Banba, 2021; Guo et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakao and Banba, 2021 and Guo et al., 2023.

claim: Picrotoxinin, isolated from Anamirta cocculus fruit, is the oldest natural NCA and is toxic to houseflies.

evidence: Supported by citation to Tong et al., 2023.

evidence: Supported by citations to Hainzl et al., 1998 and Tanaka, 2019.

evidence: Supported by citations to Sheng et al., 2018 and Li et al., 2021.

evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about competitive antagonists.
